tip: Тот, кто (tot, kto) means he who: the pointer тот (tot = that one) leads and the relative кто (kto = who) opens the clause.
In reported questions Russian keeps the original tense: живу (zhivu = live) stays present after спросила (sprosila = asked), where English might shift to lived.
с (s = with) takes the instrumental case, so молоко (moloko) becomes молоком (molokom): чай с молоком (chai s molokom = tea with milk).
пока не (poka ne = until) marks the point an action lasts up to. The не (ne) here is not a negation: стемнело (stemnelo = it got dark) is a real event.
если (esli = if) here is a real condition. For an unreal one use если бы plus a past verb: если бы ты хотел (esli by ty khotel = if you wanted).
As a conjunction раз (raz) means since or given that, a casual way to give a reason: Раз ты здесь (raz ty zdes = since you are here).
The imperfective past читал (chital = used to read) covers repeated action, so with каждый день (kazhdy den = every day) it means read habitually.
надела (nadela = put on) comes from надеть (nadet), for putting clothes on yourself. одеть (odet) means to dress someone else. Платье (plate = dress) takes надеть.
куда (kuda = to where) marks direction with a motion verb like едем (edem = we go). Use где (gde = where) only for a fixed location.
сказали (skazali = told) with no subject plus dative мне (mne = to me) is Russian's they-told-me, standing in for the English passive I was told.
After как только (kak tolko = as soon as) Russian uses a future verb: освобожусь (osvobozhus = I will be free), where English keeps the present.
The verb бояться (boyatsya = to fear) takes the genitive, so the relative is чего (chego), not что (chto): то, чего я боялся (to, chego ya boyalsya = what I feared).
так что (tak chto = so, therefore) marks a result: уехали, так что дом пустой (uekhali, tak chto dom pustoy). For a cause use так как (tak kak) instead.
The frame как ... так и (kak ... tak i) means both...and: Как дети, так и взрослые (kak deti, tak i vzroslye = both children and adults).
Paired не только ... но и (ne tolko ... no i) means not only...but also: не только он, но и она (ne tolko on, no i ona = not only he, but she).
как бы ... ни (kak by ... ni) means no matter how: Как бы трудно ни было (kak by trudno ni bylo = however hard it is). The ни (ni) is not a negation.
чтобы (chtoby) marks a wish or command and takes a past-tense verb: чтобы мы были (chtoby my byli = that we be). Plain что (chto = that) only reports a fact.
The preposition stays before который (kotory): по которому (po kotoromu = along which). Russian never strands по (po) at the end the way English does.
